title: Refutation Two-Chance: A New Frontier for Pop-Up Debate
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart reports on adapting Les Lynn's Refutation Two-Chance structure to his pop-up debates as the next step when students plateau in argument quality. He recounts two trials. The first, on who started the Cold War, went badly because students were unused to rounds and points, forgot the counter-argument, and he judged refutations clumsily. The second, on nuclear weapons, went far better after he scaffolded, required flow note-taking for everyone, and modeled it on the projector. He credits clearer arguments and note-taking for easier judging and greater participation. The post is a candid teacher case study of iterating on an instructional routine, closing with a plan to introduce it earlier next year.
points: Refutation Two-Chance is a harder variant of pop-up debate suited to students whose argumentative work has plateaued.
The first attempt failed for three fixable reasons: too little scaffolding, no note-taking, and the teacher judging fuzzy refutations too quickly.
Requiring every student to flow the debate and modeling it live gives everyone work to do and produces clearer arguments.
Naming the benefits of challenge and the class mantra 'do hard things' helped students persist through discomfort.
Refutation is called one of the twin pillars of argumentation, so Stuart plans to bring the structure in earlier in the year.
quotes: The best pop-up debates I've ever facilitated were at the end of last school year when I applied Les' rigorous Refutation Two-Chance to pop-up debates, and they were the best because they were hard. I knew it was hard because, where my outspoken students typically beg for pop-up debates, after our first Refutation Two-Chance these students were asking, “Can we just do it the old way?

Weeping and gnashing of teeth. Kids were frustrated for a variety of reasons: - First, they weren't used to points in pop-up debates or to the existence of “rounds” or to the general idea of sticking to one argument before moving on to another one. This made the comfortable kids uncomfortable and the kids with a fear of public speaking pretty scared.

Second, by the time they got to the second chance at refutation, most kids in the room had forgotten the counter-argument and the argument. This made refutation really hard. - Solution: Next time, we would all take notes.

Third, I had rarely “judged” their debate performances live before and never with points on the line, and so I was super clunky in working through whether a counter-argument had been adequately refuted or not.
I saw a vast improvement in student participation, student success, and clarity of teaching as demonstrated by student learning (both when they spoke up and in the “flow” notes they took).

Second, every student had to take notes using this flow note-taking document (another of Les' tools with slight modifications by me), and I was modeling how to do that on the projector screen. As I modeled, I encouraged students not to copy me verbatim and to use abbreviations that they could make sense of. Sometimes my modeling required me to ask that a given arguer or counter-arguer clarify her work, and this started to produce clearer initial arguments and counter-arguments as the debate progressed.

I have always said that pop-up debate is simple to a fault, and one of those faults is that the pre-debate teaching and modeling can only go so far in ensuring that every student is tracking and grappling with every argument presented by students.
